transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28
Start time: 15:00 EDT
Duration: 48 minutes (scheduled)
Location: Zoom (recording enabled)
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Singh (Sable Head of IT), Ethan Cole (Infra), Lena Korhonen (Compliance), Omar Ruiz (Data Scientist)

Summary: Brief discovery for on-prem air-gapped/private deployment readiness. Focus on offline update process, hardware constraints (GPU types, storage), network restrictions, compliance (audit logs, KMS/HSM), and performance expectations. Timeline tentatively Q4 pilot.

Topics: offline update cadence, patching process for air-gapped islands, hardware SKU compatibility, KV cache / model cache persistence, backup/restore, signing of artifacts, RBAC/SSO in disconnected mode, proof-of-life benchmarks.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we'll do a short agenda — goals for today are to understand your environment and see if Redwood Private in an air-gapped setup will fit your regulatory constraints. Samir and I will take notes.
[00:08] Dr. Maya Singh: Hi, Maya here. Thanks for doing this. We're... uh, trying to get clarity on how to keep inference inside our facility and still be able to do updates without internet.
[00:15] Ethan Cole: Ethan — infra. we maintain two racks of A100s and a smaller farm of T4s for inference testing. All outbound is blocked except a jump-host we control.
[00:22] Samir Gupta: Thanks — helpful. Do you have a hardware inventory doc we can poke at? Even SKU-level is fine.
[00:28] Ethan Cole: Yeah, I can share. It's not 100% up to date but it'll do.
[00:30] Omar Ruiz: Omar here — primary use is model serving for clinical NLP and document summarization. Latency target for patient-facing features is sub-350ms at p95. Cost is a secondary concern but throughput matters for batch jobs.
[00:45] Alex Chen: Great. A few quick questions on constraints: 1) Are you allowed to accept signed artifacts via USB or do you require on-prem airgap transfer only through a specific appliance? 2) Who manages keys — do you have an HSM/KMS on site?
[01:00] Lena Korhonen: For compliance, anything that touches PHI has to stay in the data center. We can accept signed images via our secure transfer appliance — it's basically a write-once staging area. We have an HSM but it's governed by our security team and there's an approval workflow.
[01:12] Alex Chen: Perfect. So that aligns with what Redwood Private can support: we prepare signed images and manifests, customer verifies signatures, deploys. Samir, do you want to add how updates look?
[01:22] Samir Gupta: Sure. In an air-gapped flow we create a release bundle that includes the model weights (or quantized variant), the runtime container, and a signed manifest with sha256 checks. For customers with a secure staging appliance you'd pull the bundle via USB or via the appliance — then an offline attestation step verifies signatures using customer's public key. There's also an optional offline telemetry package that can be shipped back via the appliance when allowed.
[01:42] Dr. Maya Singh: When you say telemetry package, is that telemetry or logs? We can't ship raw logs outside because of PHI.
[01:49] Samir Gupta: Right — by default we don't pull any PHI. The offline package is metric-level data and process traces without payload content; think counts, latency histograms, error rates. If you need logs stripped to only metadata that's possible, but it requires a policy agreement.
[02:05] Ethan Cole: One of our big concerns is patching. Our current cadence is quarterly maintenance windows. Can Redwood support manual patching only during windows, and also we require reproducible artifact signing so we have a chain of custody.
[02:18] Alex Chen: Yes — customers can control when patches are applied. We'll provide the signed artifacts prior to your window and the deployment is manual from your side; you can choose to apply at the window. Chain of custody is via signed manifests and audit logs maintained locally.
[02:30] Lena Korhonen: Audit logs are critical. We need to retain logs for 7 years for some workflows. Does Redwood provide on-prem audit log retention or do we need to plug into our existing SIEM?
[02:40] Samir Gupta: Redwood Private writes audit events to local files or configurable endpoints. You can ship them to your SIEM; if air-gapped, we can write them to (a) local object store or (b) the secure staging appliance for secure export. Retention and rotation policies are configurable.
[02:55] Omar Ruiz: For performance — are there special kernels for the attention ops you mention in docs? We currently use a mix of FP16 and q4 quantized models. Our inference code relies on KV cache persistence between multi-turn sessions for chat features.
[03:10] Samir Gupta: Yes, the runtime uses fused attention kernels where possible and has KV cache persistence options. In air-gapped mode the kernel selection is based on the compiled runtime we ship — generally we recommend A100 with 80GB for high concurrency; for cost-sensitive spots we support int8/q4 variants on T4s but need to validate memory/latency tradeoffs.
[03:26] Ethan Cole: We only have 40GB A100s in the racks right now — is that going to be a blocker?
[03:30] Samir Gupta: Not necessarily but it changes SLOs. 40GB will limit max context and model size. We'll run a capacity estimate. We can also recommend model quantization and sharding strategies to fit. I'll put that in the follow-up.
[03:40] Dr. Maya Singh: Timeline: regulatory wants a pilot in Q4, 2026. What does Redwood need to enable a pilot?
[03:47] Alex Chen: For a Q4 pilot we typically want: hardware inventory, a small test dataset (synthetic or redacted for PHI), admin contacts for access to staging appliance, and a list of acceptance criteria — e.g., latency p95 <350ms, successful offline update process, audit log completeness. We'll prepare a pilot plan once we have that.
[04:05] Lena Korhonen: Acceptance criteria will need to include proof that no PHI leaves the environment; also verification that keys never leave HSM.
[04:12] Samir Gupta: We support integrating with on-prem HSMs for key signing and can also use customer-managed KMS for decrypting artifacts. The signing keys used by Redwood to create bundles can be replaced by keys you generate if you want to sign locally.
[04:25] Omar Ruiz: Are there any prerequisite OS/kernel versions or container runtimes you depend on? Our infra team is pretty strict about what versions are allowed.
[04:32] Samir Gupta: Minimal supported kernel is 5.15+ due to NVIDIA driver compatibility for the distributed runtime; we support Docker and containerd, and also provide an OCI image if you have a restricted runtime. We'll send a compatibility matrix.
[04:45] Ethan Cole: Network topology question: we use a dedicated mgmt VLAN that can reach the staging appliance, but the inference nodes are on an isolated VLAN with no outbound. Do you require direct node-level connectivity to a manager?
[04:56] Alex Chen: Redwood Private can operate in a manager-less mode where the control plane is offline and you manage lifecycle via the appliance. Full telemetry and automated rollouts require connectivity to a manager, but for strict air-gap we support manual push and local operator UI.
[05:10] Dr. Maya Singh: How do rollbacks work if an update causes regressions? We need an immediate rollback path and a way to validate model quality before promoting to prod.
[05:18] Samir Gupta: We sign both current and previous artifacts and provide a local canary test harness. Rollback is a manual or semi-automated action that swaps the runtime pointers to the previous image and model weights; we recommend canary on a small set before full rollout. We'll include rollback playbooks in the docs.
[05:34] Alex Chen: Also, do you have existing eval sets for quality checks? That helps define acceptance.
[05:38] Omar Ruiz: We have a redacted eval suite for summarization and a small prompt set for clinical Q&A. We can share the test harness in a sanitized form.
[05:45] Ethan Cole: Question about storage: how big are the model artifacts after quantization? We need to plan for object storage capacity and snapshot cadence.
[05:52] Samir Gupta: Quantized weights can be 4–8x smaller depending on technique. A 70B model when quantized might be in the low tens of GBs; we'll provide per-model estimates. Snapshot cadence is configurable — snapshots are recommended before any update, and we support incremental deltas for faster transfers.
[06:10] Lena Korhonen: On authentication: we enforce SAML SSO for admin access. Can Redwood integrate with our SSO for the local operator UI?
[06:17] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports SAML and can be integrated with your IdP. RBAC maps can be provisioned, and we can provide an auditor role that only reads logs.
[06:25] Dr. Maya Singh: A potential blocker is our procurement: we need a security review and an on-site audit. Is Redwood comfortable with an on-site review of the deployment process?
[06:34] Alex Chen: Absolutely — we can accommodate on-site audits and provide artifacts and staff for walkthroughs. We'll need to schedule well in advance.
[06:40] Omar Ruiz: Do you have any references for other pharma/biotech customers doing air-gapped?
[06:44] Alex Chen: We can share anonymized case studies; I'll include two reference contacts (with permission) that have similar constraints.
[06:50] Ethan Cole: Performance benchmarks — can we run a micro-benchmark in our environment to confirm latency? We'd like to run a 1-week soak with synthetic traffic.
[06:58] Samir Gupta: Yes, we can provide a benchmark harness that runs locally and reports metrics to a local file. If you can share the hardware we can precompile the runtime variants to match.
[07:10] Dr. Maya Singh: Security question: encryption at rest — do model weights need to be decrypted in memory? How do you prevent temp files or paging with sensitive content?
[07:19] Samir Gupta: We support encrypted weights and perform in-memory decryption with mlock where possible. We also avoid writing raw weights to local disk; any temporary files are encrypted and zeroed on cleanup. On systems without mlock we provide guidance.
[07:36] Ethan Cole: What about firmware updates and driver versions — do you require NVIDIA driver updates for major runtime changes? That can be a pain with our long change windows.
[07:44] Samir Gupta: Major runtime improvements sometimes require driver updates. We try to support a range of driver versions and provide compiled kernels per-driver when possible, but some optimizations require newer drivers. We'll surface that in the compatibility matrix and flag any driver bumps planned.
[07:58] Alex Chen: Are there any non‑functional constraints we haven't talked about? e.g., local backup windows, disaster recovery runbooks, or change freeze periods?
[08:06] Ethan Cole: We have a nightly backup, monthly snapshots, and a quarterly change freeze for audited workloads. Any changes during freeze need exec sign-off.
[08:14] Lena Korhonen: Also, note that for certain regulated studies we need both immutable chain-of-custody and MD5/sha audit checks maintained for every artifact transfer.
[08:23] Samir Gupta: We'll include hash verification in the bundle transfer and log those verifications in the audit trail.
[08:28] Alex Chen: Ok quick recap of next steps — Samir will create a preliminary capacity estimate for 40GB A100s and T4 fallbacks; I'll send the security whitepaper and the private deployment checklist; you folks will send hardware inventory and compliance constraints. We'll plan the SRE security deep-dive for the week of 8/10.
[08:44] Dr. Maya Singh: That matches our expectations. One last question: pricing structure — do you price private deployment as a license or per-device?
[08:51] Alex Chen: Private is typically a platform license with optional Dedicated reserved capacity add-ons. For on-prem deployments we do a base platform fee plus a per-GPU or per-instance maintenance/throughput tier. We'll send a sample term sheet.
[09:06] Ethan Cole: For procurement, we'll need a clear list of deliverables and acceptance criteria in the SOW.
[09:10] Alex Chen: Understood — we'll prepare a draft SOW for review.
[09:15] Omar Ruiz: Any immediate blockers from Redwood side?
[09:18] Samir Gupta: Nothing blocking — mostly gathering the inventory and compliance details.
[09:22] Alex Chen: OK thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and the checklist.
[09:26] Dr. Maya Singh: Thanks, talk soon.

End of recording.
